Caithness
KAYTH-nes
n. (the far northern Scottish county, Norse in speech and law for centuries, left with vast parishes and few preachers)
Old Norse Katanes, the headland of the Cat people, the Pictish tribe of that name, with nes, a promontory.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Caithness is the flat, treeless county at the extreme north-east of the Scottish mainland, divided from Sutherland by the Ord and from Orkney by the Pentland Firth. It was Norse for four centuries, held under the earls of Orkney, and its speech and law were Scandinavian long after it was nominally Scottish; the place names are Norse in the lowland east and Gaelic in the western hills. Its bishopric was at Dornoch and its cathedral burned with Bishop Adam in 1222 by men resisting his demand of tithes in butter. From the Reformation onward the county's difficulty was simple and structural: parishes of enormous extent, a scattered people, livings too poor to attract an educated minister, and patrons who presented whom they pleased. Whole districts went through generations with a reading minister or none, and the evangelical awakening reached the county late, through catechists and lay exhorters rather than through the parish system. The dictionary enters Caithness to state the famine of the Word in its exact biblical sense, and to name where the responsibility lay.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a famine as a general scarcity; a watchman as a sentinel; dumb as mute; a catechist as one who instructs by question; and a patron as one who has the gift of a benefice.

expand to see more

FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.

WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch and give notice of danger.

DUMB, a. Mute; silent; not speaking; incapable of speech or unwilling to speak.

CATECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer; one appointed to instruct in the principles of religion.

PATRON, n. One who has the gift and disposition of a church benefice; a protector or supporter.

Key Scripture

Amo 8:11 — "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:"

Hos 4:6 — "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children."

Eze 33:7 — "So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me."

Isa 56:10 — "His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber."

Modern Corruption

Far northern Scottish county, Norse in speech and law for centuries, whose enormous parishes and poor livings left whole districts for generations with a reading minister or none.

expand to see more

The corruption named here is ours and it is structural rather than doctrinal, which makes it easier to excuse and no less serious. Caithness had parishes of a size no one man could visit, stipends no educated man would take, and lay patrons who presented relatives and favourites; the result was a county nominally Protestant and practically untaught. Amos names the condition precisely, and the striking thing is that he names it as a judgment sent rather than an accident suffered: “I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11). Hosea fixes the blame where it belongs, not on the hungry but on those who had the knowledge and withheld it: “because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me” (Hos 4:6).

The second paragraph names the office that was vacant. A minister is a watchman accountable to God for warning the people in front of him, and the commission is personal and unassignable: “I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7). Isaiah's description of what such men become when the office is treated as a living is the harshest in Scripture and the dictionary quotes it against its own side: “His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber” (Isa 56:10). What eventually reached the far north was the catechist and the lay exhorter, men with a Gaelic Bible and no stipend going round the townships; the dictionary records that the system did not supply them and that God did.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra'ab (H7458), famine; Hebrew da'ath (H1847), knowledge; Hebrew tsaphah (H6822), to watch.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'ab (H7458) — famine, hunger; “I will send a famine in the land”, Amos 8:11.

Hebrew da'ath (H1847) — knowledge, perception; “because thou hast rejected knowledge”, Hosea 4:6.

Hebrew tsaphah (H6822) — to keep watch, to look out; “I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel”, Ezekiel 33:7.

Hebrew zahar (H2094) — to warn, to admonish; “and warn them from me”, Ezekiel 33:7.

Hebrew 'illem (H483) — dumb, unable to speak; “they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark”, Isaiah 56:10.

Usage

"“but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11) — parishes no one man could visit."

"“because thou hast rejected knowledge” (Hos 4:6) — the blame on those who withheld it."

"“they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark” (Isa 56:10) — quoted against our own side."
